en: Having set aside his turban, fly-whisk, and parasol, as well as his sword, jewels, and sandals,
he bowed down properly with palms joined in reverence.
Prasenajit asks the Lord of the World:
[1] Regarding the Tathāgatas who have entered final nirvāṇa— those whose intentions are for the welfare [of beings] and whose very nature is compassion—
Having performed worship to the One of Foremost Wisdom, how might mortals obtain happiness in future existences, O Foremost Wisdom? [2]
The Blessed One Nṛsiṃha, whose eye is direct regarding all phenomena throughout the past and the future,
[spoke] then in the presence of Ānandabhadra.
The Tathāgata spoke this question:
"O King, listen today to the requested matter, concerning how one should perform worship after making a vow to the Jinas."
In other births, mortals obtain this manifold and vast ripening;
it is desirable and diverse.
Endowed with beauty, charm, and virtuous qualities, their senses guarded and their splendor like that of the sun,
they become a delight to the eyes in this world.
Those who here cause an image of the Jina to be made,
their body becomes stainless,
liberated from all diseases, fears, and sorrows.
He who fashions an image of the Sugata, as delicate as the interior of a lotus and magnificent,
shall never fall into servitude nor into a state of poverty.
Neither servitude nor low birth,
nor even any deficiency of the sense faculties shall befall one who makes an image of the Lord of the World. [7]
Having honored the image of the Sage with noble garlands and showers of flowers,
those humans become [deities] in the world of gods and men.
Well-adorned, with variegated and pleasing voices,
their sorrows vanished, their limbs firm,
possessing excellent enjoyments and treasuries of many jewels.
Mortals indeed become conquerors of the hosts of enemies after having caused a stūpa of the Lord of Munis to be built,
and by practicing the supreme conduct that accords with the Dharma. [9]
Indeed, through the offering of a staff at the shrine of the Victor, one attains morality, learning, patience, and even every accomplishment in this world. [10]
Those who have been born among gods or even among mortals with limbs as firm as those of Nārāyaṇa become endowed with qualities worthy of honor.
By offering a series of parasols upon the most excellent stupas,
one’s entire body becomes forever free from the fire of grief and disease; such persons are always happy and possessed of great wealth.
Having plastered the reliquary of the Lord of Munis with white lime in the worlds of gods and humans, they shall become long-lived,
their words authoritative, and endowed with great fame. [12]
Those who offer bells at the shrine of the Jina become possessors of the memory of past lives, utterers of the sound of Brahman, and charming; their bodies become adorned with various wonders. [13]
With their limbs adorned by necklaces, half-necklaces, bracelets, and excellent armlets,
they indeed wander through this world as attendants of the Teacher.
And they hang pendants upon the shrines;
and being joyful, they offer various kinds of magnificent parasols at the shrine of the Sugata.
In the world of gods and humans,
they become lords of gods and lords of men,
like parasols adorned with bands of shining gold and silver. [15]
For by having a stūpa built for the Lord of Sages,
mortals come to possess radiant splendor and beautiful, well-formed bodies in other future existences. [16]
For he who has placed his faith in the shrine of the Sugata, that performer of meritorious deeds indeed bears upon his head a golden garland variegated with many jewels.
A mortal who constructs a flower-garland monastery,
having attained and experienced the supreme splendor of a lord of men as well as the highest bliss of a lord of gods, [attains liberation]. [17]
He obtains the distinguished fillet of liberation, bound as a crown upon the stūpa of the Sugata; his body is anointed with perfumes and adorned with various sandalwood pastes. [18]
They become radiant with a brilliance like that of the sun,
those who apply an ointment of oil mixed with the finest perfumes at the stūpa of the Sugata. [19]
Having offered sublime fragrances, prepared with many ingredients— such as black aloe-wood, sandalwood, and saffron—
at the stupa of the Sugata, one gives this magnificent gift.
Their entire bodies become honored with fragrances;
they hear sweet and pleasing sounds, the notes of flutes, and delightful songs.
And they attain the analytical knowledges who praise the excellent relic-element of the Jina; others likewise uphold that relic-element.
Abounding in profound, logical, and radiant eloquence, their pleasing speech is perfected with the five factors;
they fill the worlds with their voice.
By the offering of musical instruments at the stūpa of a Jina,
one becomes possessed of delicate skin, a complexion like gold,
free from envy, and endowed with all virtues.
Those who cover a stūpa of the Jina with cloth, being clothed in modesty, become doers of merit;
their eyes will be like the petals of a fully blossomed blue lotus.
Having offered a lamp at the shrine of the Peerless One, they come to possess serene, gentle, long, and beautiful faces, and divine, stainless eyes. [24]
Those with large blue eyes become pleasing to the sight, possessing abundant treasuries,
and are worthy of being gazed upon by both women and men.
And those who offer garlands of lamps at the shrine are neither stained by passion, nor corrupted by hatred,
nor deluded by ignorance, nor attached to wrong views.
Mortals become joyful and happy after removing the faded garlands from the shrine of the Jina;
they become beautiful to behold and pleasing to the eye. [26]
Having purified the reliquary of the Lord of Sages, they become gracious, with the complexion of a lotus petal, and are liberated from the dust of blackness. [27]
Delighted women, most excellent in their beauty, fan them with jeweled fans that have golden handles.
Those who, during the summer season, settle the dust in the courtyard of a stūpa with pure water,
will have their wounds healed and their bodies become smooth and pure.
Those who apply coatings of clay and cow dung at the stūpas of the Sugata become endowed with happiness in the worlds of gods and humans. [29]
Mortals wandering through the realms of existence obtain lion-thrones and excellent seats,
those who [give] to virtuous groups of ascetics.
They provide beds and seats.
Those who provide noble food, suitable for renunciants, to the Saṅghas; [30] they provide it.
Those who have entered the wilderness of saṃsāra obtain food endowed with excellent color, flavor, and so forth;
and those who have gone forth obtain drink suitable for renunciants.
They offer magnificent gifts to the Saṅghas;
those who have entered the wilderness of saṃsāra obtain beverages endowed with excellent color, flavor, and other qualities. [32]
Then, filled with joy and his countenance radiant with clarity, he circumambulated the Saṅgha and the Ṛṣi,
and having prostrated at the feet of the Lord of Munis, he paid his respects.
The lord of men departed from the Jeta Grove.
The sixth sūtra, the *Prasenajitparipṛcchā*, is completed.
